source: the annex F worked example, plus the clause 5.4 LV and TLV layouts
note: CFDP wire encodings: the modular checksum and the LV/TLV forms. The annex F checksum is one of the few genuinely published CCSDS test vectors, which is why it leads this file. LV and TLV are not self-describing — both open with an octet a decoder could read as either a length or a type — so which encoding is present is prior agreement and appears in each decode vector's config rather than its fields. The transaction state machines are not covered here.

encode.name: modular-checksum-annex-f
encode.note: The 15-octet file of annex F, octets 00 through 0e. The modular checksum sums big-endian 32-bit words with the final partial word zero-padded on the right: 0x00010203 + 0x04050607 + 0x08090a0b + 0x0c0d0e00 = 0x181c2015, modulo 2^32. The right-padding of that last word is the detail worth pinning; padding on the left would give a different sum.

encode.name: modular-checksum-empty-file
encode.note: An empty file sums nothing, so the checksum is zero. Follows from the definition.

encode.name: lv-empty
encode.note: An LV is a single length octet followed by that many value octets. Empty value: just the zero length octet.

encode.name: lv-filename
encode.note: The value 'file.dat' is 8 octets, so the length octet is 0x08 followed by the ASCII. LVs carry filenames in CFDP metadata, which is why the ASCII case is the realistic one.

encode.name: lv-maximum-length
encode.note: The length field is one octet, so 255 is the longest value an LV can carry. Length octet 0xff followed by 255 octets of 0xaa. Pins the field width: a 256-octet value has no representation.

encode.name: tlv-message-to-user
encode.note: A TLV is a type octet, a length octet, then the value. Type 0x02 is a message to user; value 'hi' is two octets. Result 02 02 68 69.

encode.name: tlv-empty-value
encode.note: A TLV with a zero-length value is still two octets: type then a zero length. A decoder that treated a zero length as end-of-list would stop early here.

decode.name: lv-filename-inverse
decode.note: The inverse of lv-filename. A decoder must report how many octets it consumed, because LVs are concatenated in a metadata PDU and the next one starts where this ended.

decode.name: lv-stops-at-its-declared-length
decode.note: The length octet says 2, so a decoder reads exactly two value octets and consumes three, leaving ff ff for whatever follows. This is what makes a sequence of LVs parseable.

decode.name: tlv-message-to-user-inverse
decode.note: The inverse of tlv-message-to-user, including the consumed count for the same reason.

reject.name: lv-value-shorter-than-its-length-octet
reject.note: The length octet says 8 but only three value octets follow. A decoder must refuse rather than return a short value or read past the buffer. A decoder must not get past octet 4: the length octet promises 8 value octets; 3 are present.

reject.name: lv-length-octet-missing
reject.note: No octets at all: not even the length is present. A decoder must not get past octet 0: no octets at all.

reject.name: tlv-value-shorter-than-its-length-octet
reject.note: Type 0x02 with a declared length of 4 but only two value octets present. A decoder must not get past octet 4: the length octet promises 4 value octets; 2 are present.

reject.name: tlv-length-octet-missing
reject.note: A type octet with no length octet after it. A decoder must not get past octet 1: the type octet reads; the length octet is absent.
